cause: Due to extreme low temperatures, a benzene lined owned by Styrolution but located on a neighboring regulated entity's property (Property owner) froze. Subsequently the increased temperature from the steam tracing caused the benzene to defrost and the line to break resulting in the a spill onto the ground and the concrete ditch. The property owner made the NRC calls. TCEQ provided the guidance to the property owner that the owner should be the one completing the STEERS notification if one was needed. Initial determination by the property owner was that the emissions from the spill were below the RQ. Subsequent information and calculations showed that there in fact was an exceedance of RQ. Since the property owner based on their initial calculation, never entered a STEERS report, Styrolution now has taken over the reporting and remediation responsibility.
actions: The neighboring regulated entity's emergency response team placed booms around the spill area and in the ditches. The outfall was closed to prevent risk of offsite impact. Emission suppressing foam was applied to the spill in the ditch. A vacuum truck was used to pick up any material spilled. The line was temporarily repaired (wrapped) to stop any further spill and is being replaced.
basis: Engineering calculations and process knowledge were used to calculate the emissions.

cause: Operations began draining a lift sump at dock and found cracked pipes; caused by the recent freeze. Initially reported to contain benzene and water, but after the analysis came back of the spilled material, it was determined to be only water and nothing else therefor no RQ's were exceeded.

cause: The PX-1 separator was found overflowing to the ditch. cause: Emissions originated from condensate liquids gathered during a planned pigging event on a 16” Tejas pipeline. Tejas utilized a separator to recover gas from the collected liquids. The recovered gas was routed to the nearby gas plant. The condensate liquids were routed to a frac tank. This pigging activity was a second run following a run conducted on August 12, 2021. The first run resulted in collection of about 10,000 gallons of condensate. Based on previous experience and knowledge of the pipeline system, liquid volumes generated in a second run should not exceed volumes generated in the first run. Therefore, Tejas expected to collect no more than 10,000 gallons of condensate liquids in the second run which would result in up to 3.6 tons of VOC emissions. However, during the second run 70,500 gallons of condensate were collected exceeding the expectations by 60,500 gallons. As a result, the event resulted in 21.9 tons of unplanned VOC emissions.
actions: For this pigging event, Tejas utilized a separator to recover gas from the collected liquids. For pigging events which are expected to generate a significant volume of liquids, Tejas will utilize emission controls such as flare to control emissions.
basis: Emissions were estimated using ProMax simulation. Parameters used in the simulation included composition of a liquid sample taken from the separator, liquids pressure and temperature, volume of collected liquids, and duration of the event.

These calculations consider the release duration, process pressure, properties of the liquid, and the size of the release area. An extended gas analysis of the light gasoline product was used to estimate mass emissions of individual pollutants. Initially, it was thought that the event resulted in an exceedance of the Reportable Quantities (RQ) for benzene; however, after reassessing release conditions, it was determined that RQs were not exceeded for any pollutant.

cause: At the start of a railcar unloading event two valves to the vent system were left open (operator error.) This resulted in the MMA Tank recirculation pump pushing liquid MMA into the vapor vent header. Eventually this pressured up the vent header causing a PSV to lift and push liquid MMA into the PSV vent header. Once exposed to atmospheric conditions this liquid evaporated and was released to the atmosphere.

cause: A spill of turbine oil (Shell Turbo S4 GX 46) was identified on-site at the APIG facility. A total of 697 gallons were released due to a failed 1" diameter tubing connection. On 7/28/2024 APIG Texas City reported a light sheen into the city drainage system.
actions: Blockage plugs and containment boom were installed on APIG Texas City site during cleaning activities to prevent migration of material into the city stormwater system. Cleaning of city piping was successfully finalized, and the city stormwater system was returned to service on 7/31/2024. APIG continues to remediate the area on-site where the spill occurred to assess soil impact and need for removal. Oily water collected form the spill is stored onsite in frac tanks and impacted soil is stored in roll off boxes awaiting disposal.
basis: APIG provided initial notification of this event on July 27, 2024, pursuant to the requirements of 30 TAC 327.3. APIG Texas City performed release calculations based on system capacity, amount of oil recovered, and the quantity of oil released is estimated as 697 gallons. Emissions to air are deemed negligible due to low vapor pressure < 0.5 Pa (20 °C / 68 °F).

cause: Unit was in process of starting up when the 100E hydrogen compressor shutdown and originally GBR thought to have exceeded SO2 limits, but upon further investigation realized the Hydrogen flow to the flare was being assumed as hydrocarbons from the unit which is not the case. Once the calculations were evaluated with this information the incident did not result in an RQ.
actions: Stabilized unit.

cause: While doing rounds, operations identified a mist leaking from the 501E reflux tower. We are still waiting on analytical to complete emissions estimates, but are reporting as much speciated VOC possible until analysis is received.
actions: Tower was isolated and unit placed in standby to stop the leak.
basis: Engineering estimates, gas chromatograph, and online flowmeter.

cause: While loading Soda Ash into a marine vessel, opacity emissions were observed exceeding 15 additional percentage points above the applicable opacity limit, averaged over a six-minute period.
actions: The material loading was completed expeditiously to minimize and stop the emissions event.

cause: While performing vegetation control in the tank farm containment area, the ground crew noticed a small leak of Crude Benzene from the tank floor of tank BW-18.
actions: A drip pan was placed at the source of the leak to contain the release and prevent ground contamination. A vacuum truck was initially used to remove the contents of the drip pan until a Vapor Scrubber Unit was able to arrive to control the emissions of the release as it was contained in the vacuum truck. The total inventory of the tank was transferred as soon as operationally possible to tank 3744 to end the event. The contents of the Vapor Scrubber Unit and vacuum truck were placed in a tote and stored in our 90-day drum storage area pending disposal.
basis: An inventory analysis from the last transfer of the tank on 04/12/25 to before the tank transfer on 04/17/25 was used to determine the quantity of product that was missing. The amount of Crude Benzene recovered via the vacuum trucks was also used to determine the quantity that was spilled. For the air emissions, AP 42 5.2.2.1.1, Eq1 and Mass Balance equation was used for the calculation.
